doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Career as leader, the Grammavision deal, and future plans
summary: Levin discusses signing with Grammavision, the difficulty of leading a band, current projects, and a hoped move to Woodstock.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: With all the things you do, if you could take a year off — not really off — and do the thing you like the best, can you nail that down? What do you really like to do the best?

It changes from year to year, decade to decade. It was in the end of the 80s I’d never signed a personal record deal before, and I did, I signed with Grammavision. And I had it in mind that I wanted to put a performing unit together and start writing some music and start fairly conventional and after five or six years try to break some new ground. I didn’t know if it was possible or if it was possible for me. But it was a scheme anyway. The Grammavision had problems and it didn’t work out. They went under after a couple of years. I think during that period it was getting harder to get a live group out there and find work. It was expensive. The tours that I did, I had to finance them. They were to promote a record but it was difficult to do. And in fact I’d been in the music scene, in the jazz scene for a long time, for many years, but when you turn the corner and you become a band leader, a solo artist, it’s kind of like starting from scratch. You know any PR that was done, it was somebody else’s PR. It’s easy to say hey I want to go to Japan, but like how many write-ups have you got in the press in Japan, not Gil Evans or the people you’re working for. So you’re kind of starting from — maybe not from square one but square two anyway. And you have to work on it. And I was getting confident through that period so it was something I felt I wanted to do. And I did it for a while and then, okay, let me go back to being a sideman. I can’t afford to be a leader. Of late, the last few years I’ve been writing more and experimenting with some projects, most of which have been either difficult or impossible to sell or to distribute publicly. At this time I think that’s something that I want to get back to, or maybe it’s some kind of a circle. I know in the 70s I was a sideman and loving it, especially hauling synthesizers and making weird noises with anybody who would let me do it. So that’s the beginning of a journey, or maybe I should have done this point earlier but I think you get to where you get when it’s time to get there. I have a lot of ideas of projects that I’d like to create or produce. I don’t know what will happen to them. This is not a great time in the history of the music business to put a record out. Record labels big and small are still trying to come to grips © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

with the technology and figure out how they’re going to turn a profit and they’re not signing things that they don’t know how they can sell. And even things that they do know how to sell they’re passing. But this is something that I want to do that I think has to come out of me, there’s actually three or four projects that I’ve already started on that I’m not sure where they’re going or what I’m going to do with them when I get to the other end but I’m going to do them anyway. Physically part of my plan is to — I was talking about Woodstock a while ago, but of just kind of moving up there and getting into the woods and just connecting with the art community up there, because there’s a lot of opportunities to just take it easy and develop stuff. And I think it’s time for me to cast off some of the pressures I’ve been under, just being in Manhattan and maintaining a studio and it’s $450 a month to garage my car. I love New York but it’s an expensive place to keep a car.
